title: NoSQL and Modern Databases: Beyond the Relational Model

questions.question: Which NoSQL family is MongoDB the best-known example of?
questions.rationale: MongoDB stores flexible JSON-like documents fetched whole, without joins — the signature of a document store. Redis is the key-value icon, Cassandra the column-family one, and Neo4j the graph leader.

questions.question: In the CAP theorem, the letter P stands for:
questions.rationale: P is partition tolerance — surviving network splits between nodes. Since partitions inevitably occur in distributed systems, the real-time choice is between consistency (C) and availability (A) when a partition strikes.

questions.question: A system that always answers queries during a network partition, possibly with stale data, is choosing:
questions.rationale: Answering at all times means favouring Availability over Consistency during a partition — the AP choice, as in Cassandra and CouchDB. CP systems like HBase may refuse requests to preserve consistency.

questions.question: Which store is the most natural fit for a shopping-cart cache needing microsecond reads?
questions.rationale: Carts are small values fetched by a single key — the exact shape a key-value store like Redis optimises, often serving entirely from memory at microsecond latency.

questions.question: 'Find all friends of friends of Ravi who reviewed a product his sister bought' is most naturally served by:
questions.rationale: Multi-hop relationship walks are graph databases' home turf: nodes and edges are traversed directly in constant hops per relationship. The same query in SQL becomes a chain of recursive JOINs that degrades quickly.

questions.question: Eventual consistency means:
options: Replicas may temporarily disagree but converge once the network heals
Writes are acknowledged only after all replicas confirm
Only one replica ever receives a write
questions.rationale: AP systems allow replicas to drift during partitions and reconcile later — 'eventually' all reads return the last written value. It trades staleness windows for uninterrupted availability.

questions.question: Cassandra's design is tuned primarily for:
options: Relentless write throughput across many machines
questions.rationale: Column-family stores like Cassandra partition rows across clusters and excel at append-heavy, partition-friendly workloads: time-series, telemetry, and messaging — explicitly not joins, which they do not support.

questions.question: BASE, the relaxed counterpart of ACID, expands to:
options: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
questions.rationale: BASE = Basically Available (answers even during partitions), Soft state (state may shift as replicas converge), Eventual consistency (agreement arrives with time). It is the design philosophy behind many NoSQL stores.

questions.question: NewSQL databases such as Google Spanner and CockroachDB aim to deliver:
options: SQL and ACID with horizontal scale
Schema-less design with strict two-phase locking
questions.rationale: NewSQL keeps the relational model and its ACID guarantees while distributing data across machines using consensus protocols (Raft/Paxos) — SQL's correctness with NoSQL's scale.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform uses PostgreSQL for orders, Redis for carts, MongoDB for the catalogue, and Neo4j for recommendations. This mix is called:
questions.rationale: Polyglot persistence means choosing several purpose-fit stores per workload rather than forcing one database to do everything — ACID for money, key-value for speed, documents for flexibility, graphs for relationships.
